tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.

- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Whenever the options differ in what happens afterward — an interface, a stored format, a default, a dependency, work that would have to be redone — the comparison goes in chat, before you ask. That message has three parts, in this order: 1. **The fork**, in one sentence: what actually differs between the options, not what they are named. 2. **One line per option**: what it buys, what it costs, and what it rules out later. Say which choices are cheap to change afterward and which are not. 3. **Your recommendation**, and the reason you hold it. Send that message. Then ask with the normal selection widget — short labels, one line of description each, your recommended option first. The message is how they decide; the widget is how they answer. You send both, and you fold neither into the other. If the options differ only in what they are called — a name, an ordering, a wording — ask directly. 271	| `--shadow-4` | `0 16px 48px rgb(15 23 42 / 0.18)` | Dialogs |

276	|---|---|---|
277	| `--z-base` | 0 | Page content |
278	| `--z-sticky` | 100 | Sticky headers and footers |

304	| `--bp-sm` | 480px | 4 | 16px | 20px |
305	| `--bp-md` | 768px | 8 | 24px | 32px |
306	| `--bp-lg` | 1024px | 12 | 24px | 40px |
307	| `--bp-xl` | 1280px | 12 | 32px | 48px |

310	## Borders, icons, and opacity

313	|---|---|---|
314	| `--border-width-hairline` | 1px | Dividers, panel outlines, input borders |
315	| `--border-width-thick` | 2px | Focus rings, selected cards, invalid inputs |
316	| `--border-width-heavy` | 4px | The active-tab indicator and left accents on banners |
317	| `--icon-xs` | 12px | Inline with caption text |

319	| `--icon-md` | 20px | Default for buttons and inputs |
320	| `--icon-lg` | 24px | Navigation and empty-state accents |
321	| `--icon-xl` | 40px | Empty-state illustrations |
322	| `--opacity-disabled` | 0.48 | Only for imagery; disabled text uses `--text-disabled` |
323	| `--opacity-scrim` | 0.48 | Dialog scrim in the light theme |
324	| `--opacity-hover-overlay` | 0.04 | Hover overlay on images and avatars |
325	| `--opacity-pressed-overlay` | 0.08 | Pressed overlay on images and avatars |
326	
327	## Data visualization
328	
329	Charts use a separate categorical sequence so that series never borrow state
330	colors (a red series reads as an error). Use the sequence in order; past eight
331	series, group the remainder into "Other".
332	
333	| Token | Light | Dark | Order |
334	|---|---|---|---|
335	| `--chart-1` | `blue-600` | `blue-400` | First series |
336	| `--chart-2` | `teal-600` | `teal-400` | Second series |
337	| `--chart-3` | `violet-600` | `violet-400` | Third series |
338	| `--chart-4` | `amber-600` | `amber-400` | Fourth series |
339	| `--chart-5` | `pink-600` | `pink-400` | Fifth series |
340	| `--chart-6` | `cyan-700` | `cyan-300` | Sixth series |
341	| `--chart-7` | `indigo-700` | `indigo-300` | Seventh series |
342	| `--chart-8` | `slate-500` | `slate-400` | Eighth series, and "Other" |
343	| `--chart-grid` | `slate-200` | `slate-800` | Gridlines |
344	| `--chart-axis` | `slate-500` | `slate-400` | Axis labels and ticks |
345	| `--chart-sequential-low` | `blue-50` | `blue-950` | Low end of a heatmap |
346	| `--chart-sequential-high` | `blue-800` | `blue-300` | High end of a heatmap |
347	
348	## Token use by surface
349	
350	The table below is the reference reviewers use when they check a surface.
351	Every cell names the token; nothing in a page stylesheet should contradict it.
352	
353	| Surface | Background | Border | Text | Radius | Shadow | Padding |
354	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
355	| Page | `--surface-page` | none | `--text-primary` | `--radius-none` | `--shadow-0` | `--space-11` |
356	| Panel | `--surface-panel` | `--border-subtle` | `--text-primary` | `--radius-lg` | `--shadow-1` | `--space-8` |
357	| Card | `--surface-panel` | `--border-subtle` | `--text-primary` | `--radius-lg` | `--shadow-1` | `--space-6` |
358	| Input | `--surface-panel` | `--border-default` | `--text-primary` | `--radius-md` | `--shadow-0` | `--space-4` `--space-5` |
359	| Read-only field | `--surface-sunken` | `--border-subtle` | `--text-secondary` | `--radius-md` | `--shadow-0` | `--space-4` `--space-5` |
360	| Menu | `--surface-raised` | `--border-subtle` | `--text-primary` | `--radius-lg` | `--shadow-3` | `--space-2` |
361	| Dialog | `--surface-raised` | none | `--text-primary` | `--radius-xl` | `--shadow-4` | `--space-8` |
362	| Toast | `--surface-inverse` | none | `--text-inverse` | `--radius-lg` | `--shadow-3` | `--space-5` `--space-6` |
363	| Tooltip | `--surface-inverse` | none | `--text-inverse` | `--radius-sm` | `--shadow-2` | `--space-2` `--space-4` |
364	| Table header | `--surface-sunken` | `--border-default` | `--text-secondary` | `--radius-none` | `--shadow-0` | `--space-4` `--space-6` |
365	| Table row | `--surface-panel` | `--border-subtle` | `--text-primary` | `--radius-none` | `--shadow-0` | `--space-4` `--space-6` |
366	| Banner | state `-subtle` | none | state `-text` | `--radius-md` | `--shadow-0` | `--space-5` `--space-6` |
367	| Sticky footer | `--surface-panel` | `--border-subtle` | `--text-primary` | `--radius-none` | `--shadow-2` | `--space-5` `--space-8` |

# 01 Foundations

These are the design tokens every page under `public/` draws from. Pages
reference tokens through CSS custom properties declared in the shared token
sheet; a raw hex value, pixel size, or duration in a page stylesheet is a
review comment. When a value you need is missing, add a token here first, then
reference it.

Tokens come in two layers. Palette tokens name a raw value and never carry
meaning. Semantic tokens name a role (surface, border, text, accent, state) and
point at a palette token per theme. Page CSS uses semantic tokens; palette
tokens appear only in this file and in the token sheet.

## Color palette

Twelve hues, eleven steps each. Steps below 500 are tints for surfaces and
borders; 500 is the reference fill; steps above 500 are for text and pressed
states. Contrast pairs that pass WCAG AA are listed under Semantic colors; do

## Semantic colors

Each semantic token resolves to a palette token per theme. The dark theme is
not shipped yet, but its column is maintained so that pages written today do
not need a second pass.

| Token | Light | Dark | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--surface-page` | `slate-50` | `slate-950` | The page background behind every panel |
| `--surface-panel` | `#ffffff` | `slate-900` | Primary content panels |
| `--surface-raised` | `#ffffff` | `slate-800` | Menus, popovers, dialogs |
| `--surface-sunken` | `slate-100` | `slate-950` | Wells, code blocks, read-only fields |
| `--surface-hover` | `slate-100` | `slate-800` | Row and item hover |
| `--surface-selected` | `blue-50` | `blue-900` | Selected rows, active navigation items |
| `--surface-inverse` | `slate-900` | `slate-50` | Tooltips, toasts |
| `--border-subtle` | `slate-200` | `slate-800` | Dividers between related items |
| `--border-default` | `slate-300` | `slate-700` | Input borders, panel outlines |
| `--border-strong` | `slate-400` | `slate-600` | Borders that must read at a glance |
| `--border-focus` | `blue-500` | `blue-400` | Focus ring, 2px, offset 2px |
| `--text-primary` | `slate-900` | `slate-50` | Body text, headings |
| `--text-secondary` | `slate-600` | `slate-300` | Helper text, metadata |
| `--text-tertiary` | `slate-500` | `slate-400` | Placeholders, timestamps |
| `--text-disabled` | `slate-400` | `slate-600` | Disabled labels and values |
| `--text-inverse` | `#ffffff` | `slate-900` | Text on inverse and filled surfaces |
| `--text-link` | `blue-600` | `blue-400` | Inline links |
| `--text-link-hover` | `blue-700` | `blue-300` | Inline link hover |
| `--accent-fill` | `blue-600` | `blue-500` | Primary buttons, checked controls |
| `--accent-fill-hover` | `blue-700` | `blue-400` | Primary button hover |
| `--accent-fill-pressed` | `blue-800` | `blue-300` | Primary button pressed |
| `--accent-subtle` | `blue-50` | `blue-950` | Accent backgrounds, info banners |
| `--danger-fill` | `red-600` | `red-500` | Destructive buttons |
| `--danger-fill-hover` | `red-700` | `red-400` | Destructive button hover |
| `--danger-text` | `red-700` | `red-300` | Error messages, invalid field text |
| `--danger-subtle` | `red-50` | `red-950` | Error banners, invalid field background |
| `--warning-text` | `amber-800` | `amber-300` | Warning messages |
| `--warning-subtle` | `amber-50` | `amber-950` | Warning banners |
| `--success-text` | `green-700` | `green-300` | Success messages |
| `--success-subtle` | `green-50` | `green-950` | Success banners |
| `--info-text` | `blue-700` | `blue-300` | Informational messages |
| `--info-subtle` | `blue-50` | `blue-950` | Informational banners |
| `--overlay-scrim` | `slate-900` at 48% | `slate-950` at 64% | Behind dialogs |

Approved contrast pairs (AA for body text): `--text-primary` on every surface
token; `--text-secondary` on `--surface-page`, `--surface-panel`,
`--surface-raised`; `--text-inverse` on `--accent-fill`, `--danger-fill`,
`--surface-inverse`. `--text-tertiary` passes AA only for large text and is
never used for content a user must read to complete a task.

## Spacing

One scale, used for padding, gaps, and margins alike. Steps are named by index,
not by size, so that the scale can be retuned without renaming.

| Token | rem | px | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--space-0` | 0 | 0 | Resetting inherited spacing |
| `--space-1` | 0.125 | 2 | Hairline offsets, icon nudges |
| `--space-2` | 0.25 | 4 | Gap between an icon and its label |
| `--space-3` | 0.375 | 6 | Padding inside badges and chips |
| `--space-4` | 0.5 | 8 | Gap between a label and its control |
| `--space-5` | 0.75 | 12 | Vertical gap between stacked fields |
| `--space-6` | 1 | 16 | Padding inside inputs and small cards |
| `--space-7` | 1.25 | 20 | Gap between buttons in a button row |
| `--space-8` | 1.5 | 24 | Padding inside panels |
| `--space-9` | 2 | 32 | Gap between panels |
| `--space-10` | 2.5 | 40 | Page gutter on tablet |
| `--space-11` | 3 | 48 | Page gutter on desktop |
| `--space-12` | 4 | 64 | Top margin above a page title |
| `--space-13` | 5 | 80 | Empty-state padding |
| `--space-14` | 6 | 96 | Marketing sections only |
| `--space-15` | 8 | 128 | Marketing sections only |

## Typography

One family for interface text and one for code. Sizes are set in rem so they
follow the user's browser setting.

| Role | Token | Size (rem) | Line height | Weight | Tracking |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Display | `--type-display` | 2.25 | 1.15 | 700 | -0.02em |
| Page title | `--type-title` | 1.5 | 1.25 | 650 | -0.01em |
| Heading 2 | `--type-h2` | 1.25 | 1.3 | 600 | -0.005em |
| Heading 3 | `--type-h3` | 1.0625 | 1.35 | 600 | 0 |
| Heading 4 | `--type-h4` | 0.9375 | 1.4 | 600 | 0.01em |
| Body large | `--type-body-lg` | 1.0625 | 1.6 | 400 | 0 |
| Body | `--type-body` | 0.9375 | 1.55 | 400 | 0 |
| Body small | `--type-body-sm` | 0.8125 | 1.5 | 400 | 0.005em |
| Label | `--type-label` | 0.875 | 1.4 | 500 | 0 |
| Caption | `--type-caption` | 0.75 | 1.4 | 400 | 0.01em |
| Overline | `--type-overline` | 0.6875 | 1.3 | 600 | 0.08em |
| Code | `--type-code` | 0.8125 | 1.5 | 400 | 0 |

Families: `--font-sans` is `"Inter", system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI",
sans-serif`; `--font-mono` is `"JetBrains Mono", ui-monospace, "SF Mono",
Menlo, monospace`. Numbers in tables use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums`.

## Radii

| Token | Value | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `--radius-none` | 0 | Tables, full-bleed surfaces |
| `--radius-sm` | 4px | Badges, checkboxes, small inputs |
| `--radius-md` | 6px | Inputs, buttons |
| `--radius-lg` | 8px | Panels, cards |
| `--radius-xl` | 12px | Dialogs |
| `--radius-full` | 9999px | Pills, avatars, switches |

## Elevation

| Token | Value | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `--shadow-0` | none | Flat surfaces |
| `--shadow-1` | `0 1px 2px rgb(15 23 42 / 0.06)` | Panels on the page background |
| `--shadow-2` | `0 2px 6px rgb(15 23 42 / 0.08)` | Raised cards, sticky headers |
| `--shadow-3` | `0 8px 24px rgb(15 23 42 / 0.12)` | Menus, popovers |
| `--shadow-4` | `0 16px 48px rgb(15 23 42 / 0.18)` | Dialogs |

## Layers

| Token | Value | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `--z-base` | 0 | Page content |
| `--z-sticky` | 100 | Sticky headers and footers |
| `--z-dropdown` | 200 | Menus and popovers |
| `--z-overlay` | 300 | Dialog scrims |
| `--z-dialog` | 310 | Dialogs |
| `--z-toast` | 400 | Toasts |
| `--z-tooltip` | 500 | Tooltips |

## Motion

| Token | Value | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `--duration-instant` | 50ms | Checkbox and switch state changes |
| `--duration-fast` | 120ms | Hover and focus transitions |
| `--duration-base` | 200ms | Expanding and collapsing |
| `--duration-slow` | 320ms | Dialogs entering |
| `--ease-standard` | `cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1)` | Most transitions |
| `--ease-enter` | `cubic-bezier(0, 0, 0, 1)` | Elements entering |
| `--ease-exit` | `cubic-bezier(0.3, 0, 1, 1)` | Elements leaving |

Every transition is disabled under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`.

## Breakpoints and grid

| Token | Min width | Columns | Gutter | Page margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--bp-xs` | 0 | 4 | 16px | 16px |
| `--bp-sm` | 480px | 4 | 16px | 20px |
| `--bp-md` | 768px | 8 | 24px | 32px |
| `--bp-lg` | 1024px | 12 | 24px | 40px |
| `--bp-xl` | 1280px | 12 | 32px | 48px |
| `--bp-2xl` | 1536px | 12 | 32px | auto, content capped at 1280px |

## Borders, icons, and opacity

| Token | Value | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `--border-width-hairline` | 1px | Dividers, panel outlines, input borders |
| `--border-width-thick` | 2px | Focus rings, selected cards, invalid inputs |
| `--border-width-heavy` | 4px | The active-tab indicator and left accents on banners |
| `--icon-xs` | 12px | Inline with caption text |
| `--icon-sm` | 16px | Inline with body text, inside small buttons |
| `--icon-md` | 20px | Default for buttons and inputs |
| `--icon-lg` | 24px | Navigation and empty-state accents |
| `--icon-xl` | 40px | Empty-state illustrations |
| `--opacity-disabled` | 0.48 | Only for imagery; disabled text uses `--text-disabled` |
| `--opacity-scrim` | 0.48 | Dialog scrim in the light theme |
| `--opacity-hover-overlay` | 0.04 | Hover overlay on images and avatars |
| `--opacity-pressed-overlay` | 0.08 | Pressed overlay on images and avatars |

## Data visualization

Charts use a separate categorical sequence so that series never borrow state
colors (a red series reads as an error). Use the sequence in order; past eight
series, group the remainder into "Other".

| Token | Light | Dark | Order |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--chart-1` | `blue-600` | `blue-400` | First series |
| `--chart-2` | `teal-600` | `teal-400` | Second series |
| `--chart-3` | `violet-600` | `violet-400` | Third series |
| `--chart-4` | `amber-600` | `amber-400` | Fourth series |
| `--chart-5` | `pink-600` | `pink-400` | Fifth series |
| `--chart-6` | `cyan-700` | `cyan-300` | Sixth series |
| `--chart-7` | `indigo-700` | `indigo-300` | Seventh series |
| `--chart-8` | `slate-500` | `slate-400` | Eighth series, and "Other" |
| `--chart-grid` | `slate-200` | `slate-800` | Gridlines |
| `--chart-axis` | `slate-500` | `slate-400` | Axis labels and ticks |
| `--chart-sequential-low` | `blue-50` | `blue-950` | Low end of a heatmap |
| `--chart-sequential-high` | `blue-800` | `blue-300` | High end of a heatmap |

## Token use by surface

The table below is the reference reviewers use when they check a surface.
Every cell names the token; nothing in a page stylesheet should contradict it.

| Surface | Background | Border | Text | Radius | Shadow | Padding |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Page | `--surface-page` | none | `--text-primary` | `--radius-none` | `--shadow-0` | `--space-11` |
| Panel | `--surface-panel` | `--border-subtle` | `--text-primary` | `--radius-lg` | `--shadow-1` | `--space-8` |
| Card | `--surface-panel` | `--border-subtle` | `--text-primary` | `--radius-lg` | `--shadow-1` | `--space-6` |
| Input | `--surface-panel` | `--border-default` | `--text-primary` | `--radius-md` | `--shadow-0` | `--space-4` `--space-5` |
| Read-only field | `--surface-sunken` | `--border-subtle` | `--text-secondary` | `--radius-md` | `--shadow-0` | `--space-4` `--space-5` |
| Menu | `--surface-raised` | `--border-subtle` | `--text-primary` | `--radius-lg` | `--shadow-3` | `--space-2` |
| Dialog | `--surface-raised` | none | `--text-primary` | `--radius-xl` | `--shadow-4` | `--space-8` |
| Toast | `--surface-inverse` | none | `--text-inverse` | `--radius-lg` | `--shadow-3` | `--space-5` `--space-6` |
| Tooltip | `--surface-inverse` | none | `--text-inverse` | `--radius-sm` | `--shadow-2` | `--space-2` `--space-4` |
| Table header | `--surface-sunken` | `--border-default` | `--text-secondary` | `--radius-none` | `--shadow-0` | `--space-4` `--space-6` |
| Table row | `--surface-panel` | `--border-subtle` | `--text-primary` | `--radius-none` | `--shadow-0` | `--space-4` `--space-6` |
| Banner | state `-subtle` | none | state `-text` | `--radius-md` | `--shadow-0` | `--space-5` `--space-6` |
| Sticky footer | `--surface-panel` | `--border-subtle` | `--text-primary` | `--radius-none` | `--shadow-2` | `--space-5` `--space-8` |

1	# 04 Content and accessibility
2	
3	How the interface talks, and the accessibility bar every page clears before it
4	ships.
5	
6	## Voice
7	
8	Plain, direct, and calm. Write the way a helpful colleague would say it out
9	loud. Lead with what the user can do, not with what went wrong. Prefer short
10	sentences and common words; cut any word that does not change the meaning.
11	
12	- Address the user as "you". Refer to the product as "we" only in messages
13	  where we did something ("We sent a code to your email").
14	- Never blame the user. "That code has expired" rather than "You entered an
15	  expired code".
16	- No exclamation marks outside of genuinely celebratory moments, and there are
17	  very few of those in a settings page.
18	- No jargon the user did not introduce. "Sign in", not "authenticate".
19	
20	## Capitalization and punctuation
21	
22	- Sentence case everywhere: page titles, headings, labels, buttons, menu items,
23	  tab names, and table headers. Proper nouns keep their capitals.
24	- Buttons are verbs or verb phrases: "Save", "Regenerate token", "Discard".
25	  Never "OK" or "Yes" in a Dialog; repeat the action.
26	- No period at the end of a label, button, heading, or single-sentence hint.
27	  Use periods in messages and multi-sentence help.
28	- Use the serial comma. Use an en dash for ranges ("9–5") and an em dash with
29	  no spaces for breaks in a sentence, sparingly.
30	
31	## Terminology
32	
33	Use the preferred term; reviewers flag the avoided forms.
34	
35	| Preferred | Avoid | Notes |
36	|---|---|---|
37	| sign in | log in, login (as a verb), authenticate | "Sign-in" as a noun or adjective |
38	| sign out | log out, logout | "Sign-out" as a noun |
39	| sign up | register, create login | Only on the public site |
40	| account | profile (for account-level settings) | Profile means the public-facing identity |
41	| profile | account (for public-facing identity) | Display name and avatar live here |
42	| settings | preferences, options, configuration | One word for every settings surface |
43	| display name | username, handle, nickname | There are no usernames in this product |
44	| email address | e-mail, mail, email ID | "Email" alone is fine in a label |
45	| time zone | timezone, TZ | Two words |
46	| language | locale | Locale is an implementation term |
47	| theme | appearance mode, skin | Light, Dark, Match system |
48	| notifications | alerts, messages | Alerts are a different, admin-only feature |
49	| email notifications | email alerts | Matches the field label |
50	| push notifications | mobile alerts, device notifications | Only for the mobile app and browser push |
51	| weekly digest | weekly summary, newsletter | Not a marketing email |
52	| two-factor authentication | 2FA, MFA, two-step verification | "Two-factor auth" in tight labels |
53	| recovery codes | backup codes | Shown once at setup |
54	| session timeout | idle timeout, auto logout | Minutes of inactivity before sign-out |
55	| API token | API key, access token, secret | Shown once, then masked |
56	| regenerate | reset, rotate, refresh | For tokens and codes |
57	| delete | remove, erase | Delete is permanent; remove is for detaching |
58	| remove | delete (when nothing is destroyed) | Removing a member keeps their account |
59	| save | apply, submit, update | For forms with a Save button |
60	| cancel | abort, back | Leaves without saving |
61	| discard | throw away, lose | Only for unsaved changes |
62	| dialog | modal, popup | In documentation; never shown to users |
63	| banner | alert bar, notice | In documentation |
64	| toast | snackbar, notification | In documentation |
65	| required | mandatory, compulsory | "(required)" after a label |
66	| optional | not required | "(optional)" after a label |
67	| invalid | wrong, bad, incorrect | In documentation; messages describe the fix |
68	| expired | timed out | For codes and sessions |
69	| offline | disconnected, no connection | In messages |
70	| workspace | organization, team, tenant | The billing and membership unit |
71	| member | user (inside a workspace) | User is fine in documentation |
72	| owner | admin (for the billing owner) | Admins are a separate role |
73	| admin | administrator, superuser | Short form everywhere |
74	
75	## Formats
76	
77	| Value | Format | Example (en-US) | Notes |
78	|---|---|---|---|
79	| Date | Locale medium date | Sep 14, 2026 | Never numeric-only in the interface |
80	| Date and time | Locale medium date, short time | Sep 14, 2026, 3:05 PM | Show the time zone when it differs from the user's |
81	| Relative time | Rounded, past only | 5 minutes ago | Switch to an absolute date after 7 days |
82	| Duration | Largest two units | 1 hr 20 min | Never "80 minutes" |
83	| Number | Locale grouping | 12,480 | Tabular figures in tables |
84	| Percentage | Up to one decimal | 12.5% | No space before % in en-US |
85	| Currency | Locale currency format | $1,250.00 | Always two decimals |
86	| File size | Binary units, one decimal | 2.4 MB | Use MB, not MiB, in the interface |
87	| Time zone | Zone name with UTC offset | Pacific Time (UTC−07:00) | Use the minus sign, not a hyphen |
88	| Phone | National format when local, else E.164 | (555) 010-4477 | Store E.164 |
89	
90	## Accessibility checklist
91	
92	Every page clears every row before it ships. "How to check" is what reviewers
93	actually do.
94	
95	| Criterion | Level | Requirement | How to check |
96	|---|---|---|---|
97	| 1.1.1 Non-text content | A | Every meaningful image and icon has a text alternative; decorative ones are hidden | Inspect alt and aria-hidden on every img and svg |
98	| 1.3.1 Info and relationships | A | Headings, lists, tables, labels, and fieldsets are real elements, not styled divs | Read the page with styles disabled |
99	| 1.3.2 Meaningful sequence | A | DOM order matches visual order | Tab through the page and watch the focus order |
100	| 1.3.3 Sensory characteristics | A | Instructions do not rely on shape, position, or color alone | Read every instruction out of context |
101	| 1.3.4 Orientation | AA | Works in portrait and landscape | Rotate a tablet emulator |
102	| 1.3.5 Identify input purpose | AA | Personal-data fields carry autocomplete tokens | Check against the field table in 03 Forms |
103	| 1.4.1 Use of color | A | Color is never the only way to convey state | View in grayscale |
104	| 1.4.3 Contrast (minimum) | AA | 4.5:1 for body text, 3:1 for large text | Use only the approved pairs in 01 Foundations |
105	| 1.4.4 Resize text | AA | Usable at 200% browser zoom without loss | Zoom to 200% and complete the main task |
106	| 1.4.5 Images of text | AA | No text rendered as images | Search the page for text in img |
107	| 1.4.10 Reflow | AA | No horizontal scrolling at 320 CSS px wide | Set the viewport to 320px |
108	| 1.4.11 Non-text contrast | AA | 3:1 for control borders and focus indicators | Check input borders and the focus ring |
109	| 1.4.12 Text spacing | AA | No clipping with increased letter, word, and line spacing | Apply the text-spacing bookmarklet |
110	| 1.4.13 Content on hover or focus | AA | Tooltips are dismissible, hoverable, and persistent | Hover, then move into the tooltip, then press Escape |
111	| 2.1.1 Keyboard | A | Every action is reachable and operable by keyboard | Unplug the mouse |
112	| 2.1.2 No keyboard trap | A | Focus can always leave a component | Tab into and out of every widget |
113	| 2.4.1 Bypass blocks | A | A skip link reaches the main content | Press Tab once on load |
114	| 2.4.2 Page titled | A | The document title names the page and the product | Check the browser tab |
115	| 2.4.3 Focus order | A | Focus moves in a logical order | Tab through and note every jump |
116	| 2.4.4 Link purpose | A | Link text makes sense out of context | List every link and read it alone |
117	| 2.4.6 Headings and labels | AA | Headings and labels describe their content | Read the heading outline alone |
118	| 2.4.7 Focus visible | AA | The focus ring is always visible | Tab through on every surface color |
119	| 2.4.11 Focus not obscured | AA | Sticky headers and footers never hide the focused element | Tab to fields near the sticky footer |
120	| 2.5.3 Label in name | A | The accessible name contains the visible label | Compare labels with the accessibility tree |
121	| 2.5.7 Dragging movements | AA | Anything draggable has a non-drag alternative | Try every drag interaction by keyboard |
122	| 2.5.8 Target size | AA | Targets are at least 24 by 24 CSS px | Measure IconButtons and checkboxes |
123	| 3.1.1 Language of page | A | The html element has a lang attribute | Inspect the root element |
124	| 3.2.1 On focus | A | Focus never triggers a change of context | Tab through every field |
125	| 3.2.2 On input | A | Changing a field never navigates or submits on its own | Change every select and radio |
126	| 3.3.1 Error identification | A | Errors are identified in text | Submit the form empty |
127	| 3.3.2 Labels or instructions | A | Every field has a label and needed instructions | Read the field table in 03 Forms |
128	| 3.3.3 Error suggestion | AA | Error messages say how to fix the problem | Compare against the message catalog |
129	| 3.3.4 Error prevention | AA | Destructive and financial actions are confirmable | Trigger every delete and regenerate |
130	| 3.3.7 Redundant entry | A | Previously entered information is not requested again | Walk the longest flow twice |
131	| 3.3.8 Accessible authentication | AA | No cognitive test to sign in; paste is allowed | Paste into every password and code field |
132	| 4.1.2 Name, role, value | A | Custom widgets expose correct roles and states | Inspect switches, tabs, and accordions |
133	| 4.1.3 Status messages | AA | Toasts and inline status are announced without moving focus | Listen with a screen reader on save |
134	
135	## Component accessibility reference
136	
137	What every shared component from 02 Components must expose, and how reviewers
138	check it. A component that fails a row here fails review regardless of how it
139	looks.
140	
141	### Button
142	
143	| Criterion | Requirement | How to check |
144	|---|---|---|
145	| Role | Exposes button | Inspect the accessibility tree in browser dev tools |
146	| Accessible name | Named by its label text | Compare the computed name with the visible text |
147	| Keyboard | Enter and Space activate | Operate it with the keyboard alone, mouse unplugged |
148	| Focus | Visible ring from 01 Foundations on :focus-visible; never removed | Tab to it on every surface color |
149	| State | aria-busy while loading | Change its state and listen with VoiceOver and NVDA |
150	| Target size | 24 by 24 px; 36 px tall at md | Measure the hit area in dev tools |

158	| Keyboard | Enter and Space activate | Operate it with the keyboard alone, mouse unplugged |

160	| State | aria-pressed when it toggles | Change its state and listen with VoiceOver and NVDA |

169	| Keyboard | Typing edits; Enter submits the form | Operate it with the keyboard alone, mouse unplugged |
170	| Focus | Visible ring from 01 Foundations on :focus-visible; never removed | Tab to it on every surface color |
171	| State | aria-invalid and aria-describedby for the message | Change its state and listen with VoiceOver and NVDA |

173	
174	### Textarea
175	
176	| Criterion | Requirement | How to check |
177	|---|---|---|
178	| Role | Exposes textbox with aria-multiline | Inspect the accessibility tree in browser dev tools |
179	| Accessible name | Named by the visible label via for and id | Compare the computed name with the visible text |
180	| Keyboard | Enter inserts a line break | Operate it with the keyboard alone, mouse unplugged |

186	
187	| Criterion | Requirement | How to check |

190	| Accessible name | Named by the visible label | Compare the computed name with the visible text |
191	| Keyboard | Space or Enter opens; arrows move; Escape closes | Operate it with the keyboard alone, mouse unplugged |

193	| State | aria-expanded and aria-activedescendant | Change its state and listen with VoiceOver and NVDA |

196	### Checkbox
197	
198	| Criterion | Requirement | How to check |
199	|---|---|---|
200	| Role | Exposes checkbox | Inspect the accessibility tree in browser dev tools |
201	| Accessible name | Named by the label to its right | Compare the computed name with the visible text |
202	| Keyboard | Space toggles | Operate it with the keyboard alone, mouse unplugged |
203	| Focus | Visible ring from 01 Foundations on :focus-visible; never removed | Tab to it on every surface color |
204	| State | aria-checked, including mixed | Change its state and listen with VoiceOver and NVDA |
205	| Target size | 24 by 24 px including the label hit area | Measure the hit area in dev tools |

213	| Keyboard | Space toggles | Operate it with the keyboard alone, mouse unplugged |
214	| Focus | Visible ring from 01 Foundations on :focus-visible; never removed | Tab to it on every surface color |

218	### RadioGroup

223	| Accessible name | Named by the fieldset legend | Compare the computed name with the visible text |
224	| Keyboard | Arrows move and select; Tab leaves the group | Operate it with the keyboard alone, mouse unplugged |
225	| Focus | Visible ring from 01 Foundations on :focus-visible; never removed | Tab to it on every surface color |
226	| State | aria-checked on each item | Change its state and listen with VoiceOver and NVDA |
227	| Target size | 24 by 24 px per item including the label | Measure the hit area in dev tools |
228	
229	### Card
230	
231	| Criterion | Requirement | How to check |
232	|---|---|---|
233	| Role | Exposes region when it has a title, otherwise none | Inspect the accessibility tree in browser dev tools |
234	| Accessible name | Named by its heading via aria-labelledby | Compare the computed name with the visible text |
235	| Keyboard | Not focusable itself | Operate it with the keyboard alone, mouse unplugged |
236	| Focus | Visible ring from 01 Foundations on :focus-visible; never removed | Tab to it on every surface color |
237	| State | none | Change its state and listen with VoiceOver and NVDA |
238	| Target size | Not applicable | Measure the hit area in dev tools |
239	
240	### Tabs
241	
242	| Criterion | Requirement | How to check |
243	|---|---|---|
244	| Role | Exposes tablist, tab, and tabpanel | Inspect the accessibility tree in browser dev tools |
245	| Accessible name | Named by each tab's label | Compare the computed name with the visible text |
246	| Keyboard | Arrows move; Enter selects in manual mode | Operate it with the keyboard alone, mouse unplugged |
247	| Focus | Visible ring from 01 Foundations on :focus-visible; never removed | Tab to it on every surface color |
248	| State | aria-selected and aria-controls | Change its state and listen with VoiceOver and NVDA |
249	| Target size | 36 px tall tabs | Measure the hit area in dev tools |
250	
251	### Accordion
252	
253	| Criterion | Requirement | How to check |
254	|---|---|---|
255	| Role | Exposes button headers controlling regions | Inspect the accessibility tree in browser dev tools |
256	| Accessible name | Named by the header text | Compare the computed name with the visible text |
257	| Keyboard | Enter and Space toggle | Operate it with the keyboard alone, mouse unplugged |
258	| Focus | Visible ring from 01 Foundations on :focus-visible; never removed | Tab to it on every surface color |
259	| State | aria-expanded and aria-controls | Change its state and listen with VoiceOver and NVDA |
260	| Target size | Full header width, 40 px tall | Measure the hit area in dev tools |
261

# 04 Content and accessibility

How the interface talks, and the accessibility bar every page clears before it
ships.

## Voice

Plain, direct, and calm. Write the way a helpful colleague would say it out
loud. Lead with what the user can do, not with what went wrong. Prefer short
sentences and common words; cut any word that does not change the meaning.

- Address the user as "you". Refer to the product as "we" only in messages
  where we did something ("We sent a code to your email").
- Never blame the user. "That code has expired" rather than "You entered an
  expired code".
- No exclamation marks outside of genuinely celebratory moments, and there are
  very few of those in a settings page.
- No jargon the user did not introduce. "Sign in", not "authenticate".

## Capitalization and punctuation

- Sentence case everywhere: page titles, headings, labels, buttons, menu items,
  tab names, and table headers. Proper nouns keep their capitals.
- Buttons are verbs or verb phrases: "Save", "Regenerate token", "Discard".
  Never "OK" or "Yes" in a Dialog; repeat the action.
- No period at the end of a label, button, heading, or single-sentence hint.
  Use periods in messages and multi-sentence help.
- Use the serial comma. Use an en dash for ranges ("9–5") and an em dash with
  no spaces for breaks in a sentence, sparingly.

## Terminology

Use the preferred term; reviewers flag the avoided forms.

| Preferred | Avoid | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| sign in | log in, login (as a verb), authenticate | "Sign-in" as a noun or adjective |
| sign out | log out, logout | "Sign-out" as a noun |
| sign up | register, create login | Only on the public site |
| account | profile (for account-level settings) | Profile means the public-facing identity |
| profile | account (for public-facing identity) | Display name and avatar live here |
| settings | preferences, options, configuration | One word for every settings surface |
| display name | username, handle, nickname | There are no usernames in this product |
| email address | e-mail, mail, email ID | "Email" alone is fine in a label |
| time zone | timezone, TZ | Two words |
| language | locale | Locale is an implementation term |
| theme | appearance mode, skin | Light, Dark, Match system |
| notifications | alerts, messages | Alerts are a different, admin-only feature |
| email notifications | email alerts | Matches the field label |
| push notifications | mobile alerts, device notifications | Only for the mobile app and browser push |
| weekly digest | weekly summary, newsletter | Not a marketing email |
| two-factor authentication | 2FA, MFA, two-step verification | "Two-factor auth" in tight labels |
| recovery codes | backup codes | Shown once at setup |
| session timeout | idle timeout, auto logout | Minutes of inactivity before sign-out |
| API token | API key, access token, secret | Shown once, then masked |
| regenerate | reset, rotate, refresh | For tokens and codes |
| delete | remove, erase | Delete is permanent; remove is for detaching |
| remove | delete (when nothing is destroyed) | Removing a member keeps their account |
| save | apply, submit, update | For forms with a Save button |
| cancel | abort, back | Leaves without saving |
| discard | throw away, lose | Only for unsaved changes |
| dialog | modal, popup | In documentation; never shown to users |
| banner | alert bar, notice | In documentation |
| toast | snackbar, notification | In documentation |
| required | mandatory, compulsory | "(required)" after a label |
| optional | not required | "(optional)" after a label |
| invalid | wrong, bad, incorrect | In documentation; messages describe the fix |
| expired | timed out | For codes and sessions |
| offline | disconnected, no connection | In messages |
| workspace | organization, team, tenant | The billing and membership unit |
| member | user (inside a workspace) | User is fine in documentation |
| owner | admin (for the billing owner) | Admins are a separate role |
| admin | administrator, superuser | Short form everywhere |

## Formats

| Value | Format | Example (en-US) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Date | Locale medium date | Sep 14, 2026 | Never numeric-only in the interface |
| Date and time | Locale medium date, short time | Sep 14, 2026, 3:05 PM | Show the time zone when it differs from the user's |
| Relative time | Rounded, past only | 5 minutes ago | Switch to an absolute date after 7 days |
| Duration | Largest two units | 1 hr 20 min | Never "80 minutes" |
| Number | Locale grouping | 12,480 | Tabular figures in tables |
| Percentage | Up to one decimal | 12.5% | No space before % in en-US |
| Currency | Locale currency format | $1,250.00 | Always two decimals |
| File size | Binary units, one decimal | 2.4 MB | Use MB, not MiB, in the interface |
| Time zone | Zone name with UTC offset | Pacific Time (UTC−07:00) | Use the minus sign, not a hyphen |
| Phone | National format when local, else E.164 | (555) 010-4477 | Store E.164 |

## Accessibility checklist

Every page clears every row before it ships. "How to check" is what reviewers
actually do.

| Criterion | Level | Requirement | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.1.1 Non-text content | A | Every meaningful image and icon has a text alternative; decorative ones are hidden | Inspect alt and aria-hidden on every img and svg |
| 1.3.1 Info and relationships | A | Headings, lists, tables, labels, and fieldsets are real elements, not styled divs | Read the page with styles disabled |
| 1.3.2 Meaningful sequence | A | DOM order matches visual order | Tab through the page and watch the focus order |
| 1.3.3 Sensory characteristics | A | Instructions do not rely on shape, position, or color alone | Read every instruction out of context |
| 1.3.4 Orientation | AA | Works in portrait and landscape | Rotate a tablet emulator |
| 1.3.5 Identify input purpose | AA | Personal-data fields carry autocomplete tokens | Check against the field table in 03 Forms |
| 1.4.1 Use of color | A | Color is never the only way to convey state | View in grayscale |
| 1.4.3 Contrast (minimum) | AA | 4.5:1 for body text, 3:1 for large text | Use only the approved pairs in 01 Foundations |
| 1.4.4 Resize text | AA | Usable at 200% browser zoom without loss | Zoom to 200% and complete the main task |
| 1.4.5 Images of text | AA | No text rendered as images | Search the page for text in img |
| 1.4.10 Reflow | AA | No horizontal scrolling at 320 CSS px wide | Set the viewport to 320px |
| 1.4.11 Non-text contrast | AA | 3:1 for control borders and focus indicators | Check input borders and the focus ring |
| 1.4.12 Text spacing | AA | No clipping with increased letter, word, and line spacing | Apply the text-spacing bookmarklet |
| 1.4.13 Content on hover or focus | AA | Tooltips are dismissible, hoverable, and persistent | Hover, then move into the tooltip, then press Escape |
| 2.1.1 Keyboard | A | Every action is reachable and operable by keyboard | Unplug the mouse |
| 2.1.2 No keyboard trap | A | Focus can always leave a component | Tab into and out of every widget |
| 2.4.1 Bypass blocks | A | A skip link reaches the main content | Press Tab once on load |
| 2.4.2 Page titled | A | The document title names the page and the product | Check the browser tab |
| 2.4.3 Focus order | A | Focus moves in a logical order | Tab through and note every jump |
| 2.4.4 Link purpose | A | Link text makes sense out of context | List every link and read it alone |
| 2.4.6 Headings and labels | AA | Headings and labels describe their content | Read the heading outline alone |
| 2.4.7 Focus visible | AA | The focus ring is always visible | Tab through on every surface color |
| 2.4.11 Focus not obscured | AA | Sticky headers and footers never hide the focused element | Tab to fields near the sticky footer |
| 2.5.3 Label in name | A | The accessible name contains the visible label | Compare labels with the accessibility tree |
| 2.5.7 Dragging movements | AA | Anything draggable has a non-drag alternative | Try every drag interaction by keyboard |
| 2.5.8 Target size | AA | Targets are at least 24 by 24 CSS px | Measure IconButtons and checkboxes |
| 3.1.1 Language of page | A | The html element has a lang attribute | Inspect the root element |
| 3.2.1 On focus | A | Focus never triggers a change of context | Tab through every field |
| 3.2.2 On input | A | Changing a field never navigates or submits on its own | Change every select and radio |
| 3.3.1 Error identification | A | Errors are identified in text | Submit the form empty |
| 3.3.2 Labels or instructions | A | Every field has a label and needed instructions | Read the field table in 03 Forms |
| 3.3.3 Error suggestion | AA | Error messages say how to fix the problem | Compare against the message catalog |
| 3.3.4 Error prevention | AA | Destructive and financial actions are confirmable | Trigger every delete and regenerate |
| 3.3.7 Redundant entry | A | Previously entered information is not requested again | Walk the longest flow twice |
| 3.3.8 Accessible authentication | AA | No cognitive test to sign in; paste is allowed | Paste into every password and code field |
| 4.1.2 Name, role, value | A | Custom widgets expose correct roles and states | Inspect switches, tabs, and accordions |
| 4.1.3 Status messages | AA | Toasts and inline status are announced without moving focus | Listen with a screen reader on save |

## Component accessibility reference

What every shared component from 02 Components must expose, and how reviewers
check it. A component that fails a row here fails review regardless of how it
looks.

### Button

| Criterion | Requirement | How to check |
|---|---|---|
| Role | Exposes button | Inspect the accessibility tree in browser dev tools |
| Accessible name | Named by its label text | Compare the computed name with the visible text |
| Keyboard | Enter and Space activate | Operate it with the keyboard alone, mouse unplugged |
| Focus | Visible ring from 01 Foundations on :focus-visible; never removed | Tab to it on every surface color |
| State | aria-busy while loading | Change its state and listen with VoiceOver and NVDA |
| Target size | 24 by 24 px; 36 px tall at md | Measure the hit area in dev tools |

| Target size | 28 px square minimum | Measure the hit area in dev tools |

### TextInput

| Focus | Visible ring from 01 Foundations on :focus-visible; never removed | Tab to it on every surface color |

1	---
2	name: brainstorming
3	description: "You MUST use this before any creative work - creating features, building components, adding functionality, or modifying behavior. Explores user intent, requirements and design before implementation."
4	---
5	
6	# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs
7	
8	Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.
9	
10	Start by classifying how much process the request needs, then work
11	through your path: understand the context, refine the idea, present a
12	design, and get your human partner's approval.
13	
14	<HARD-GATE>
15	Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any
16	project, or take any implementation action until you have told your
17	human partner what you intend and they have approved it. This applies
18	to EVERY task on EVERY path below — the ceremony scales with the task;
19	the approval gate never does.
20	</HARD-GATE>
21	
22	**REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use hyperpowers:communication for everything your human partner reads on every path: the questions, the approach comparison, the design presentation, and the spec.
23	
24	**After every context compaction:** Claude Code re-attaches this skill cut to its first 20,000 characters, which ends before the spec-writing steps, and a full Read you made before the compaction does not survive it. After each compaction, the first and every later one, Read this file in full before your next action (a question to your human partner, a visual-companion step, or writing the spec), along with any other skill you are following whose re-attached copy is cut short.
25	
26	## Three Paths
27	
28	Before your first question, classify the request and say the
29	classification out loud — "this looks bounded, so I'll present a short
30	design here rather than write a spec" — so your human partner can
31	override it:
32	
33	- **Spike** — a feasibility question ("can we...", "is it possible...",
34	  "quick and dirty is fine") whose output is an answer, not code you
35	  keep. Present the question and what you'll try in 2-3 sentences, get
36	  a nod, then find out as cheaply as correctness allows. No design
37	  doc, no spec file. Report findings as a recommendation; anything you
38	  built stays labeled throwaway.
39	- **Bounded** — a well-scoped change to code that already exists in
40	  this repo: a new flag, a small endpoint, a one-file fix.
41	  Understanding the kind of app is not enough — bounded means the flow
42	  you are changing is already here to read. If there is no existing
43	  flow to change, the task is not bounded. Classify by the outcome the
44	  request names, not by the code your first edit would touch: if the
45	  request names structure this repo does not have — a new module or
46	  layer, a new subsystem such as logging or storage, reuse across
47	  components that do not exist yet — the flow you would be changing is
48	  not already here, however small the first edit looks, and the task
49	  is architectural. Choosing between algorithms or options inside a
50	  function that already exists names no new structure and stays
51	  bounded. Ask the clarifying questions that matter, present a short
52	  design IN CHAT (a few sentences to a few short paragraphs), and
53	  STOP. Implementation starts only after your human partner says yes
54	  to that design — a bounded task's approval is as hard a gate as an
55	  architectural one. No spec file, no implementation plan document.
56	- **Architectural** — new projects, new subsystems, changes that
57	  restructure how components fit together or alter interfaces others
58	  depend on. Follow the full process: questions, approaches, sectioned
59	  design, written spec, then the writing-plans skill.
60	
61	When in doubt between two paths, take the heavier one. The ratchet is
62	one-way: hidden complexity discovered mid-task upgrades the path —
63	stop, say so, and step up. Nothing downgrades mid-task.
64	
65	## Anti-Pattern: "Too Simple To Need Approval"
66	
67	Every path ends with your human partner approving your intent before
68	implementation. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config
69	change — the design may be two sentences in chat, but you MUST present
70	it and get approval. "Simple" tasks are where unexamined assumptions
71	cause the most wasted work. What scales with simplicity is the
72	artifact, never the approval.
73	
74	## Red Flags
75	
76	| Thought | Reality |
77	|---------|---------|
78	| "This is too simple to need a design" | Simple means a short design, not no design. Two sentences in chat, then approval. |
79	| "I'll call it bounded and skip the spec" | Reaching for a label to skip work IS the doubt — take the heavier path. |
80	| "It's bounded and the design is obvious — I'll start while they read it" | The gate is the approval, not the design's length. Present, then stop until you hear yes. |
81	| "I understand this kind of app, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the repo, not your familiarity. A new project has no existing flow — it is architectural. |
82	| "The code I'd touch is right here, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the outcome's shape, not the entry point. A request naming a new module, a new subsystem, or reuse across components that do not exist yet is architectural even when the edit starts in one file. |
83	| "The spike works, so I'll keep the code" | A spike's output is an answer. Keeping the code is a new request — classify it. |
84	| "It grew, but I'm almost done — no need to re-classify" | Hidden complexity upgrades the path mid-task. Stop and say so. |
85	| "They approved the spike, so the follow-up change is approved too" | Each task gets its own classification and its own approval. |
86	| "It's bounded, so the visual companion doesn't apply" | The companion keys on the question being visual, not on the path being heavy. Open it — the task stays bounded. |
87	
88	## Checklist
89	
90	Classify first, announce the path, then create a task for each item on
91	your path and complete them in order.
92	
93	**Spike:**
94	1. **Explore project context** — enough to frame the probe
95	2. **Present question + probe plan** — 2-3 sentences
96	3. **Get approval** — a nod is enough
97	4. **Investigate** — as cheaply as correctness allows (The approach gate's any-path trigger applies here too — explicit request or genuinely material alternatives fire it; feasibility probes rarely do.)
98	5. **Report findings** — a recommendation; label anything built as throwaway
99	
100	**Bounded:**
101	1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
102	2. **Visual companion (conditional)** — if a question here would genuinely be clearer shown than described (a layout, a diagram, side-by-side options), open it just-in-time. Ceremony does not escalate: the design still lands in chat. See the Visual Companion section below.
103	3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, the ones that matter
104	4. **Codex approach gate (conditional)** — if the design space has real architectural, algorithmic, or data-model alternatives, or your human partner asks for Codex input, run [codex-approach-gate.md](codex-approach-gate.md) and fold its approaches into the short in-chat design with provenance tags. Ceremony does not escalate. Trivial/mechanical bounded tasks skip this silently.
105	5. **Present short design in chat** — approach, files touched, testing
106	6. **Get approval** — STOP and wait for an explicit yes; presenting the design and starting in the same breath is skipping the gate
107	7. **Implement** — proceed with the normal development workflow (TDD applies); no plan document
108	
109	**Architectural:**
110	1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
111	2. **Use the visual companion just-in-time** — NOT upfront. The first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than described, open it then and tell the user what you're doing — no separate approval gate. If no visual question ever arises, never open it. See the Visual Companion section below.
112	3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
113	4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation. Before finalizing them, run [codex-approach-gate.md](codex-approach-gate.md) if the approach gate fires (rule below) and fold its approaches into this step with provenance tags.
114	5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
115	6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/hyperpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` (do not commit unless the user asks)
116	7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
117	8. **Codex spec review gate** (Claude Code only) — run the Codex review gate over the spec before involving the user (see below)
118	9. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
119	10. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan
120	
121	**Codex approach gate (conditional, Claude Code only):** the gate's trigger is
122	path-independent — real architectural, algorithmic, or data-model
123	alternatives, or your human partner asking for Codex input, fire it on any
124	path. On the bounded path its approaches fold into the short in-chat design;
125	ceremony does not escalate. On the spike path it does not normally fire
126	(feasibility probes rarely present committed design alternatives), but an
127	explicit request or genuinely material alternatives still fire it.
128	Trivial/mechanical tasks skip it silently.
129	
130	**Visual companion (conditional, any path):** its trigger is path-independent
131	too — the first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than
132	described, open it, whichever path you are on. Adding or moving something on a
133	page or screen always raises one: where it goes. Show the placements in the
134	companion before you present the design. Classification does not gate it:
135	a bounded task that opens the companion is still bounded and still ends in a
136	short in-chat design, and a spike that sketches one screen is still a spike.
137	What fires it is the question being visual, not the path being heavy. If no
138	visual question ever arises, never open it.
139	
140	## Process Flow
141	
142	```dot
143	digraph brainstorming {
144	    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" [shape=diamond];
145	    "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" [shape=box];
146	    "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" [shape=box];
147	    "Real architecture/algorithm/data-model choices\nor partner requests Codex? (bounded)" [shape=diamond];
148	    "Codex approach gate (one-shot); fold into\nshort design (no escalation)" [shape=box];
149	    "Present short design in chat" [shape=box];
150	    "Human approves?" [shape=diamond];
151	    "Investigate; report recommendation" [shape=doublecircle];
152	    "Implement via normal workflow (no plan doc)" [shape=doublecircle];
153	    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
154	    "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
155	    "Real architecture/algorithm/data-model choices\nor partner requests Codex?" [shape=diamond];
156	    "Codex approach gate (one-shot)\n(Claude Code; degrade if absent)" [shape=box];
157	    "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
158	    "Present design sections" [shape=box];
159	    "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
160	    "Write design doc" [shape=box];
161	    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" [shape=box];
162	    "Codex spec gate\n(Claude Code; degrade if absent)" [shape=box];
163	    "User reviews spec?" [shape=diamond];
164	    "Invoke writing-plans skill" [shape=doublecircle];
165	    "Hidden complexity? Upgrade path" [shape=box];
166	
167	    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" [label="spike"];
168	    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" [label="bounded"];
169	    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Explore project context" [label="architectural"];
170	    "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" -> "Human approves?";
171	    "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" -> "Real architecture/algorithm/data-model choices\nor partner requests Codex? (bounded)";
172	    "Real architecture/algorithm/data-model choices\nor partner requests Codex? (bounded)" -> "Codex approach gate (one-shot); fold into\nshort design (no escalation)" [label="yes"];
173	    "Real architecture/algorithm/data-model choices\nor partner requests Codex? (bounded)" -> "Present short design in chat" [label="no - trivial"];
174	    "Codex approach gate (one-shot); fold into\nshort design (no escalation)" -> "Present short design in chat";
175	    "Present short design in chat" -> "Human approves?";
176	    "Human approves?" -> "Investigate; report recommendation" [label="spike: yes"];
177	    "Human approves?" -> "Implement via normal workflow (no plan doc)" [label="bounded: yes"];
178	    "Hidden complexity? Upgrade path" -> "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural";
179	    "Explore project context" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
180	    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Real architecture/algorithm/data-model choices\nor partner requests Codex?";
181	    "Real architecture/algorithm/data-model choices\nor partner requests Codex?" -> "Codex approach gate (one-shot)\n(Claude Code; degrade if absent)" [label="yes"];

183	    "Codex approach gate (one-shot)\n(Claude Code; degrade if absent)" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
184	    "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
185	    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
186	    "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
187	    "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
188	    "Write design doc" -> "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)";
189	    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" -> "Codex spec gate\n(Claude Code; degrade if absent)";
190	    "Codex spec gate\n(Claude Code; degrade if absent)" -> "User reviews spec?";
191	    "User reviews spec?" -> "Write design doc" [label="changes requested"];
192	    "User reviews spec?" -> "Invoke writing-plans skill" [label="approved"];
193	}
194	```
195	
196	**Terminal states are path-bound.** Architectural: the ONLY skill you
197	invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans — never frontend-design,
198	mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. Bounded: after
199	approval, implementation proceeds directly through the normal
200	development workflow; no plan document. Spike: the terminal state is a
201	reported recommendation.
202	
203	## The Process
204	
205	The subsections below serve the bounded and architectural paths (a
206	spike stops at "present the probe, get a nod"). Sections from
207	**Exploring approaches** onward are architectural-path depth — for
208	bounded work, context plus a few questions plus a short in-chat design
209	is the whole process.
210	
211	**Understanding the idea:**
212	
213	- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
214	- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
215	- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
216	- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
217	- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too. When the options differ in what happens afterward, the comparison goes in chat before you ask — see Deciding Together below
218	- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
219	- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria
220	
221	**Exploring approaches:**
222	
223	- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
224	- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
225	- Lead with your recommended option and explain why
226	- YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design
227	- **Codex approach gate (conditional):** when the design space has real architectural, algorithmic, or data-model alternatives — or your human partner explicitly asks — get Codex's independent approaches first via [codex-approach-gate.md](codex-approach-gate.md): blind handoff, one shot, approaches folded into this step with provenance tags and judged on merits, not origin.
228	
229	**Presenting the design:**
230	
231	- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
232	- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
233	- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
234	- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
235	- For a new project (or one with no configured tooling), the design presentation includes a short tooling question alongside the architecture: which of these to set up from the start — cheapest before any code exists: aggressive linting + auto-formatting (the stack's standard, e.g. ruff+format / eslint+prettier / clippy+rustfmt); unit-test infrastructure (runner, layout, a first passing fixture); end-to-end test infrastructure; fuzz or mutation testing where the stack supports it. The user's selections land in the spec's Global Constraints so every later plan and task inherits them.
236	- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense
237	
238	**Design for isolation and clarity:**
239	
240	- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
241	- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
242	- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
243	- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.
244	
245	**Working in existing codebases:**
246	
247	- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
248	- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
249	- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.
250	
251	## Deciding Together
252	
253	Five-word labels with a line of description each are plenty for "which of
254	these do you prefer" and nowhere near enough for a choice your human partner
255	has to live with. Whenever the options differ in what happens afterward — an
256	interface, a stored format, a default, a dependency, work that would have to
257	be redone — the comparison goes in chat, before you ask.
258	
259	That message has three parts, in this order:
260	
261	1. **The fork**, in one sentence: what actually differs between the options,
262	   not what they are named.
263	2. **One line per option**: what it buys, what it costs, and what it rules
264	   out later. Say which choices are cheap to change afterward and which are
265	   not.
266	3. **Your recommendation**, and the reason you hold it.
267	
268	Send that message. Then ask with the normal selection widget — short labels,
269	one line of description each, your recommended option first. The message is
270	how they decide; the widget is how they answer. You send both, and you fold
271	neither into the other.
272	
273	If the options differ only in what they are called — a name, an ordering, a
274	wording — ask directly. There is nothing to compare.
275	
276	## Visual Companion
277	
278	A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode, and not a path. Having it open means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.
279	
280	**Using the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT open it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, just use it: start the server with `--open` so the user's browser opens to the first screen, and tell them what you're doing in the same message — no separate approval gate.
281	> "I'll sketch this in a browser tab so it's easier to see — opening it now at <URL>. (It's token-intensive, so say the word if you'd rather keep things in the terminal.)"
282	
283	If a visual question never arises, never open it. If the user asks to stop using it, continue text-only and don't reopen it unless they raise it again.
284	
285	**Per-question decision:** Even with the companion open, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**
286	
287	- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
288	- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions
289	
290	A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.
291	
292	Before opening the companion for the first time, read the detailed guide:
293	`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`
294	
295	## After the Design (architectural path)
296	
297	**Documentation:**
298	
299	- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/hyperpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
300	  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
301	- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
302	- Do NOT commit the design document. Leave it as an uncommitted working file unless the user explicitly asks you to commit it.
303	- Where the design rests on something nobody confirmed, write it as
304	  `Assumption: <what>, validate via <method>` rather than as a fact; the
305	  plan will attach the deadline. The placeholder scan accepts that form
306	  and flags bare TBD or TODO.
307	
308	**Spec Self-Review:**
309	After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:
310	
311	1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
312	2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
313	3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
314	4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.
315	
316	Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.
317	
318	**Codex Spec Review Gate (Claude Code only):**
319	After the spec self-review passes and before involving the user, run the Codex
320	review gate over the spec file as a **document** review using the spec recipe.
321	Follow
322	[../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md](../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md):
323	probe availability, and if Codex is present, provide the spec path plus any
324	available approved-design context, have it review the spec, and resolve blocking
325	findings in the convergence fix loop (document-gate backstop of 4 rounds) before
326	the user review; if Codex is absent, emit the no-Codex notice and proceed. This
327	gate never blocks the user review — at worst it is skipped.
328	
329	**User Review Gate:**
330	After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:
331	
332	> "Spec written to `<path>` (not committed). Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."
333	
334	Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.
335	
336	**Implementation:**
337	
338	- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
339	- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.
340
